desc:
Given an array nums of positive integers and a non-negative integer target, decide whether some group of elements of nums adds up to exactly target. Every element (every index) may be used at most once. The empty group has sum 0, so target = 0 is always reachable.

Return true if such a group exists and false otherwise.

nums = [3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2], target = 9  -> true   (4 + 5)
nums = [3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2], target = 30 -> false
nums = [2, 4, 6, 8],         target = 7  -> false
hints: Trying every subset costs 2n, far too much. Think about which sums you can reach rather than which subsets you can build.
Keep a boolean table reach[s]: can some subset of the elements seen so far add up to s? At the start only reach[0] is true.
When an element x arrives, every reachable sum s makes s + x reachable too. Loop s from target down to x and set reach[s] |= reach[s - x]; going downward keeps the element from being used twice.
editorial: This is the 0/1 knapsack in its purest form: the only question is which totals can be formed. Let reach[s] say whether some subset of the elements processed so far sums to s. Initially only reach[0] is true (the empty subset). For a new element x, a total s becomes reachable if s - x was reachable before this element, so reach[s] = reach[s] or reach[s - x].

The loop over s has to go from high to low. Then reach[s - x] is still the value from before the current element and the element is counted at most once; a loop going upward would reuse it. Total cost is O(n · target) time and O(target) space.

A neat speed-up stores the whole table in one big integer used as a bitset: bits |= bits << x does the entire update at once, and the answer is bit number target. The reference solution does exactly that.
